strengths: Proposes a unified Product-of-Experts framework that can compose heterogeneous generative and discriminative experts at inference time without retraining.
Shows practical instantiations across image editing, video generation, and text-to-image layout composition, including integration of VLMs, graphics engines, and physics simulators.
Introduces a conditional sampling heuristic to improve MCMC mixing, with an ablation suggesting it helps visual fidelity and controllability.
Provides a flexible user interface for generation goals via text, images, poses, and trajectories, with qualitative examples demonstrating controllability.
Combines AIS/SMC with flow/diffusion models in a coherent pipeline and includes supplementary implementation details.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core ingredients (product of experts, AIS/SMC, compositional diffusion, reward steering) are well established, and the main new component is a heuristic conditional sampling approximation.

Technical soundness is questionable for the black-box discriminative expert case: MCMC moves target only the generative product, while discriminative experts are used only as resampling weights, so the algorithm may not actually sample from the stated product distribution without additional corrections.
Conditional sampling in Eq. (7) is ad hoc and lacks rigorous derivation or guarantees; the Gaussian flow-deviation justification in Appendix D.2 is an unverified approximation.

The evaluation is small-scale and incomplete: image object insertion uses only 10 images x 3 objects = 30 scenes; video uses 12 object-centric scenes plus 9 PhysGen3D scenes; text-to-image composition is largely qualitative with no quantitative table.

Baselines are limited: for image editing only RF-Solver is compared; for video, baselines are mostly variants of the same backbone; other training-free compositional and reward-steering methods are not compared.
Automatic GPT-4o evaluation and small test sets do not provide strong evidence for broad claims about controllability, fidelity, or superiority over monolithic methods.

Reproducibility is limited: the method relies on large proprietary or external models (FLUX, Wan2.1, GPT-4o, VQAScore, Genesis), high compute (4-30 minutes per sample), and no code release is mentioned.
Claims are stronger than the evidence: phrases like sampling from the product distribution and better controllability/fidelity are supported mainly by narrow experiments and qualitative examples.
The societal-impact discussion is generic and does not address misuse risks of highly controllable visual generation in depth.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: inference-time composition of heterogeneous generative and discriminative experts for visual generation.
Provides a unified probabilistic Product-of-Experts formulation that connects generative priors, VLM rewards, and physics simulators under one sampling framework.
Training-free approach avoids retraining large models and can in principle leverage existing pre-trained experts.
Uses Annealed Importance Sampling and Sequential Monte Carlo to improve sample efficiency over naive rejection sampling.
Demonstrates several applications: graphics-engine-guided image insertion, physics-simulator-guided video generation, and regional text-to-image composition.
The framework offers flexible control interfaces via different expert configurations (text, image, pose, trajectory).
Includes some quantitative evaluations and ablations, e.g., conditional sampling and particle-count comparisons, showing controllability gains on selected tasks.
Discusses compute limitations, societal impact, and leaves large-scale PoE sampling as future work.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core ingredients—Product of Experts, AIS/SMC, compositional diffusion, and reward steering—are well established, and the paper mainly combines them with heterogeneous experts rather than introducing a fundamental new algorithm.

The SMC/AIS algorithm is not fully specified or theoretically justified. Algorithm 1 omits proper importance-weight computations, and resampling based solely on discriminative rewards at intermediate steps may not correctly target the intended product distribution.
The intermediate discriminative expert construction, r_t(x)=r(\hat{x}) using endpoint prediction from the composed flow, is heuristic and lacks rigorous analysis or ablation.
The conditional sampling approximation in Eq. (7) is ad hoc and weakly justified in Appendix D.2; it is not clear that it corresponds to the stated conditional distribution.
Key experiments use L=1 particles for image and video tasks, making the SMC/discriminative-resampling contribution largely inactive; the main SMC benefits are not convincingly demonstrated.
Evaluation is small-scale and ad hoc: 30 image scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, and 9 PhysGen3D scenes, with no standard benchmark or human evaluation.
Baselines are limited: RF-Solver is not a compositional generation method, and video baselines are monolithic models; comparisons to prior compositional/reward-steering methods are missing.
Section 4.4, which uses the VLM discriminative expert and SMC, has only qualitative results and no quantitative evaluation, so central claims about discriminative composition are unsupported.
Many reported improvements are marginal or within standard deviation, and some metrics are worse than baselines (e.g., aesthetic score in image editing, ViCLIP in full-scene video).

Reproducibility is weak: no code release, reliance on large proprietary models and simulators (FLUX, Wan, GPT-4o, Genesis, PhysGen3D), and high compute requirements (4–30 minutes per sample on H200 GPUs).
Notation and presentation need improvement: overloaded use of p, unclear definition of products over heterogeneous scene spaces, incomplete algorithm sketch, and several typographical errors.

Significance is unclear: the method is demonstrated with a few experts on small datasets, and the paper itself leaves large-scale PoE sampling as future work, so impact on top-tier AI remains unproven.

strengths: Introduces a general Product-of-Experts framework for inference-time composition of heterogeneous visual generative and discriminative experts, with a training-free sampling procedure based on AIS/SMC.
Provides a practical instantiation using flow models, including composed velocity/score construction, conditional generative experts, and black-box discriminative resampling.

Demonstrates the framework across multiple visual generation tasks: graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physical-simulator-instructed video generation, and regional text-to-image composition with VLM guidance.
Includes quantitative comparisons on image and video tasks with appropriate controllability, image/video-quality metrics, standard deviations, and an ablation for conditional sampling.
The method enables flexible user control via text, image, pose, trajectory, and simulator inputs, which is a useful direction for controllable visual generation.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is small-scale and proof-of-concept: 30 image scenes, 12 object-centric video scenes, and 9 full-scene simulation videos, with no large-scale benchmark or human evaluation.

The strongest claimed benefit of integrating discriminative experts (e.g., VLM rewards) is evaluated only qualitatively on text-to-image generation; no quantitative table or systematic ablation for VLM-guided PoE is provided.

Several key components are heuristic or approximate, including the conditional sampling update in Eq. (7) and the use of black-box discriminative resampling without discriminative gradients; exactness/consistency of the AIS/SMC sampler is not rigorously established.
Baselines are limited for some tasks; e.g., image editing compares mainly to RF-Solver, and the paper does not compare to other compositional/energy-based generation or control methods.
Reproducibility is weakened by reliance on proprietary/closed models (FLUX, Wan, GPT-4o, Genesis) and no clear code/implementation release, plus high inference cost (minutes per sample).

Some claims are broader than the evidence, especially around physical accuracy and heterogeneous expert composition, since simulators are often used as conditioning signals rather than fully independent experts.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (annealing schedule, particle count, MCMC steps, conditional loss weight w) is not sufficiently ablated; sample sizes are small enough that significance of metric differences is unclear.

strengths: Introduces a unified product-of-experts framework for controllable visual generation that can combine heterogeneous generative models, discriminative VLMs, and physics simulators at inference time.
Proposes a practical AIS + SMC-style sampler with annealed MCMC and resampling, enabling black-box discriminative expert guidance without retraining.
Demonstrates flexible control interfaces and applicability across image object insertion, physics-simulator video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image generation.
Provides extensive experiments, qualitative comparisons, ablations (conditional sampling, SMC, particle budget), and implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Technical soundness of the sampler is not fully established: the MCMC kernels are described as leaving p_t invariant, but p_t includes discriminative experts that are often treated as black boxes and not incorporated into the kernel, so correctness/asymptotic guarantees are unclear; final max selection and heuristic resampling further weaken theoretical claims.
The conditional sampling approximation in Eq. (6) is heuristic and may alter the intended product distribution; its justification is deferred and not rigorously validated.

Evaluation is limited in scale: e.g., 30 image-insertion scenes, 80 character-insertion scenes, 12 video scenes, 9 full-scene simulation scenes, and 50 sampled MIG-Bench cases. This limits statistical significance and generality.

Comparisons are partly confounded by differing backbones and application-specific adaptations; several tables show mixed results where baselines outperform the proposed method on important metrics (e.g., background preservation, LPIPS).
Reliance on GPT-4o/VLM automatic metrics and no human evaluation makes the claimed gains in controllability/fidelity less reliable.
Compute cost is high (4–30 minutes per sample), so the 'efficient' framing is questionable; practical scalability to many experts/large-scale sampling remains untested.
Novelty is incremental relative to prior compositional diffusion/MCMC/SMC work; the main algorithmic difference (per-timestep MCMC kernels) needs stronger theoretical and empirical support.
No code release or reproducibility artifact is mentioned; several implementation details are in the appendix but independent verification would be nontrivial.

strengths: Proposes a unified probabilistic product-of-experts framework that can combine heterogeneous generative models, discriminative models, and physics-simulator-derived constraints without retraining.
Develops a practical AIS/SMC-style sampling procedure with black-box discriminative experts and flexible user interfaces for controllable image/video generation.
Demonstrates the framework on several tasks: graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image generation.
Includes quantitative evaluations and qualitative visualizations, plus ablations on conditional sampling, particle count, and SMC resampling.
The training-free nature and compatibility with different generative paradigms (flow, autoregressive, diffusion) are attractive properties for controllable synthesis.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: product-of-experts composition, annealed MCMC, and SMC for generative model composition are well established; the main algorithmic difference over closely related work is incremental and not rigorously shown to be substantially better.

Technical soundness is questionable: Algorithm 1 resamples particles using only discriminative-expert weights while generative transition/annealing weights are not explicitly accumulated, so exact sampling from the intended product distribution is not established. The claimed per-timestep MCMC invariance does not by itself justify the SMC weights used.

The conditional sampling approximation in Eq. (6) is heuristic, derived from flow-vector agreement rather than a principled conditional distribution, and lacks theoretical guarantees or error analysis.

Evaluation is too limited to support broad claims: several experiments use only tens of scenes, rely heavily on automatic GPT-4o/VLM metrics without human evaluation, and report large variances without significance testing.

Baselines are incomplete or potentially mismatched: important recent composition/guidance methods are missing, some comparisons use different backbones, and several tasks lack strong state-of-the-art baselines.

Reproducibility is insufficient: key hyperparameters, prompts, reward scaling, MCMC step sizes, resampling schedules, and implementation details are only partially specified; no code or model release is indicated.

The physics-simulator integration is shallow: simulator outputs are largely converted into RGB/depth/trajectory signals or a Gaussian penalty, rather than embedding physical dynamics and constraints directly into the probabilistic composition.
The paper overclaims computational efficiency and general controllability while requiring minutes per sample and validating only small-scale, narrow settings with a limited number of experts.
Clarity and presentation need improvement: some notation and equations are confusing, Algorithm 1 is hard to verify from the main text, and there are typos and formatting issues.

strengths: The paper proposes a unified probabilistic product-of-experts framework for controllable visual generation, integrating heterogeneous generative models, discriminative VLM-based rewards, and physics simulator signals at inference time without retraining.

It introduces a practical AIS/SMC-style sampler that uses per-timestep MCMC kernels and parallel particle resampling, supporting both flow/diffusion and autoregressive generative experts while requiring only black-box access to discriminative experts.

The framework is applied to several meaningful tasks: graphics-engine-guided image object insertion, physics-simulator-guided video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image generation, with flexible user interfaces for combining experts.

The experimental sections include quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, and ablations on conditional sampling, SMC resampling, particle count, and compute budget, which provide concrete evidence for the method's controllability and fidelity benefits.

The appendix gives substantial implementation detail, including flow-model instantiation, conditional sampling justification, automatic evaluation protocols, and per-task hyperparameters, supporting some reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: product-of-experts, AIS, and SMC are well-established, and the main contribution is their orchestration/instantiation for visual generation rather than a fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical result.

The evaluation is relatively small-scale across several tasks, and some baselines are not fully controlled: e.g., the first image-editing comparison uses only RF-Solver, several Magic Insert comparisons rely on different backbones or downloaded outputs, and GPT-4o-based automatic metrics can be noisy.

The conditional sampling approximation in Eq. (6) is heuristic and based on matching flow vectors with stop-gradient; it lacks rigorous theoretical guarantees and may be sensitive to the weight/learning rate and expert compatibility assumptions.

Reproducibility is limited by heavy dependence on large external models and hardware (FLUX, Wan2.1, FramePack, VQAScore, GPT-4o, H200 GPUs) and by no clear code release; per-sample run times of minutes to tens of minutes are substantial.

The claimed integration of physics simulators as probabilistic experts is only partially realized: the flow-video setting uses simulator outputs mainly as depth/trajectory conditions, while the autoregressive setting approximates the simulator distribution via MAP updates rather than true sampling.

The SMC ablation is useful but not uniformly strong, with some mIoU values decreasing as particles/resampling are added; additional comparisons against other inference-time composition or reward-steering methods would strengthen the empirical positioning.

Some algorithmic and writing details are unclear or possibly corrupted in the manuscript, including the resampling/weight update in Algorithm 1 and several equations/symbols, making it harder to verify exact correctness.
